summary: Gives examples of Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) call flows, including registration and session establishment. It shows call flow diagrams and message details among user agents, proxy servers and redirect servers. It is a best current practice document.

eli5.summary: This is a picture book showing exactly which messages Internet phones send to ring each other, step by step, so developers can check their own programs behave the same.

subtitle: A worked picture book of SIP messages: registering, calling, redirecting, and failing, with every header shown.

tldr.problem: The SIP specification in RFC 3261 is large, and implementers need concrete, reviewed examples of what the messages should look like in the most basic scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through registration and session-establishment call flows between user agents, proxy servers, a redirect server and an ALG, with numbered message diagrams (F1, F2, ...) and the full text of each message.
tldr.outcome: The flows are best-practice illustrations, not exact templates: the document itself warns that some details were deliberately simplified or made incorrect for readability and must not be copied as is.

today: RFC 3665 is a Best Current Practice document, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its examples build on RFC 3261, and PSTN interworking examples are in RFC 3666.

sections.title: Purpose and Assumptions
sections.content:
RFC 3665 (BCP 75) collects SIP call flows developed in the design of a SIP IP communications network. They represent an example minimum set of functionality, written to help implementers, designers and protocol researchers toward a standard implementation of RFC 3261. The flows are based on SIP version 2.0 with SDP usage from RFC 3264. Call flows that interwork with the PSTN through gateways are in the companion RFC 3666.

The assumptions are not requirements. User agents authenticate with HTTP Digest, some proxies insert Record-Route headers to stay in the signaling path, and the examples use TCP, TLS and UDP transport.
sections.eli5: It is a guide that shows the normal way phones talk, using made-up people, so you can compare your own phone's behaviour.

sections.title: How to Read the Flows
sections.content:
In the diagrams, dashed lines (---) are mandatory signaling messages, double dashed lines (===) are media paths, and a name in parentheses marks an optional message. Messages are labelled F1, F2 and so on, matching the message details listed after each figure, with comments written as /* ... */.

The RFC says the exact flows must not be copied as is. For readability the examples differ from real SIP: Digest responses are not real MD5 values, Call-IDs are often repeated, CSeq counts often start at 1, header fields appear in the same order, and only the minimum header set is shown (no Accept, Supported or Allow).

The cast is fixed: Alice at alice@atlanta.example.com, Bob at bob@biloxi.example.com (also bob@chicago.example.com), and proxies, a registrar and an ALG on example.com hosts with addresses in the 192.0.2.x range.
sections.eli5: The pictures are tidy cartoons of real conversations, so do not copy the made-up passwords and numbers into a real phone.

sections.title: SIP Registration
sections.content:
Registration binds a device's Contact URI to a user's Address of Record (AOR). Five flows are shown. In a new registration Bob sends REGISTER, receives a 401 Unauthorized carrying a Digest challenge, repeats the REGISTER with credentials, and gets 200 OK listing his current contacts. TLS is used because HTTP Digest lacks integrity protection and registration hijacking would otherwise be a danger.

The other flows start from an already authenticated user, so there is no challenge. An update sends a new contact list. A query is a REGISTER with no Contact headers, and the 200 OK returns the current list. A cancellation sends Expires: 0 and Contact: *, and the server clears the contact list. In the unsuccessful case the password in the second REGISTER is wrong and the server answers 401 again.
sections.eli5: Registering is telling the phone company where to find you. You show your password, and later you can change the address, ask what is on file, or cross it out.

sections.title: Basic Session Establishment
sections.content:
Section 3 sets up calls between Alice and Bob, who are assumed to be SIP phones. The successful calls show initial signaling, SDP media information, the media session and finally termination. In the simplest flow (3.1) Alice sends INVITE directly to Bob with an SDP body, Bob replies 180 Ringing then 200 OK, Alice sends ACK, RTP media flows both ways, and Bob ends the call with BYE, answered by 200 OK.

Flow 3.2 adds two proxies. Alice's INVITE carries a pre-loaded Route header for Proxy 1, which challenges with a 407; Alice resends with credentials. Both proxies add Record-Route headers so that later requests such as ACK and BYE carry Route headers and travel through them. Flow 3.3 repeats this with both proxies challenging, since Alice has valid credentials in both domains.
sections.eli5: To make a call, Alice rings Bob, Bob's phone says ringing, Bob picks up, Alice says got it, they talk, and then one of them hangs up.

sections.title: Failover, ALGs, Redirects and re-INVITE
sections.content:
Further successful scenarios cover less simple cases. In 3.4, Alice has a primary proxy and a secondary proxy (or uses DNS SRV records to find them). Proxy 1 is reachable but does not respond, so she retries and then completes the call through Proxy 2. In 3.5 the call passes through a SIP ALG (Application Layer Gateway), which terminates and bridges both media streams by rewriting the SDP. The RFC notes this Back-to-Back User Agent could also serve firewall traversal, an anonymizer, or codec conversion such as mu-law to A-law.

In 3.6 a redirect server answers 302 Moved Temporarily with Bob's current address, Alice sends a new INVITE through a proxy, and because the INVITE had no SDP the SDP is carried in the ACK. In 3.7 Bob's IP address changes mid-call, so he sends a re-INVITE with a new Contact and SDP (version number incremented) to move the media stream.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the first road is closed, the call needs a helper in the middle, the phone book says Bob has moved, or Bob changes his address during the call. Each case has its own set of messages.

sections.title: Unsuccessful Call Attempts
sections.content:
Four failure flows are shown. In no answer (3.8), Alice gives up after a 180 Ringing and sends CANCEL. Each hop acknowledges the CANCEL with a 200 OK hop by hop rather than end to end, and Bob's side then returns 487. If a 200 OK to the INVITE had crossed with the CANCEL, Alice would have sent an ACK then a BYE.

In busy (3.9) Bob sends 486 Busy Here; the non-2xx response is acknowledged hop by hop, and the RFC notes that many SIP UAs will not return a 486 because they have multiple lines. In no response (3.10) Proxy 2 retransmits the INVITE and after the sixth re-transmission gives up and sends 480 No Response. In temporarily unavailable (3.11) Bob sends 180 Ringing and then 480, which is acknowledged and passed back to Alice.
sections.eli5: Not every call works. Alice can hang up before Bob answers, Bob can be busy, Bob's phone can stay silent, or it can ring and then say he is not available.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document only gives examples, the security considerations of RFC 3261 apply. That RFC describes the basic threats: registration hijacking, server impersonation, message body tampering, session modifying or teardown, and denial of service and amplification attacks.

HTTP Digest as used here gives one-way authentication and protection against replay attacks, but it lacks integrity protection, which is why registration uses TLS. TLS together with the sips URI scheme gives better security including two-way authentication, and S/MIME can give end-to-end confidentiality and integrity for message bodies. No IANA section is present in the table of contents.
sections.eli5: Passwords alone are like whispering your secret across a crowded room. Using TLS is like moving to a private room first.
